name: Symmetric rendezvous search: certify a better bound on the line (4.1520 < R < 4.2574, unchanged since 2008) or beat the 2026 record on four locations
compute_profile: laptop-days (strategy optimisation over distributions on unit-step paths; exact rational evaluation of a candidate takes seconds to hours)
statement: Two searchers start distance 2 apart on a line. They have no common orientation and use the same synchronised random rule with independent randomness, at speed at most 1. Han, Du, Vera and Zuluaga (Operations Research 2008) give line bounds reported as 4.1520 and 4.2574. Georgiou, Gravel, Kapusin and Mandic (arXiv:2609.13632) restate them. The separate discrete-location model uses independent random labelings. Cembrano, Fischer and Klimm (arXiv:2604.02058) give an FSD strategy improving Anderson-Weber for n>=4. The target is a certified stronger line bound or a strategy beating the best exact FSD parameter choice for four locations. Printed line bars require numerical separation; a strict comparison with the exact incumbent strategy is a partial target.
success_criterion: CONFIRMED by any one of the following, with the strategy given as a finite explicit object (for the line, for example a distribution over k-step unit-move paths in the sense of Han et al., or a finite-state randomized automaton over moves -1/0/+1 in the agent's own frame; for n locations, a finite-memory randomized rule over location labels) and its expected meeting time computed exactly in rational arithmetic, or enclosed by rigorous interval arithmetic, by a verifier sharing no code with the search. (a) Line, upper bound: expected meeting time <= 4.2573 for initial distance 2 (a margin of 1e-4 below the published 4.2574, so that rounding of the old value cannot matter), counting meetings that happen mid-step. (b) Line, lower bound: a rigorous proof that every symmetric strategy has expected meeting time >= 4.1521, with the computational part (for example a rational dual certificate of an SDP or LP relaxation over a strategy class proved sufficient) checked exactly. (c) Four locations: a symmetric strategy for n = 4 whose exact expected meeting time is strictly below the minimum over theta in [0, 1) of the exact expected meeting time of the Cembrano-Fischer-Klimm strategy FSD(theta), computed from the exact expression in arXiv:2604.02058 in that paper's time convention (meetings possible from t = 0). In each case the value must beat every bound published at verification time (check arXiv for 'symmetric rendezvous'). The line margins compare against rounded numerical bars. The exact-incumbent comparison in p1 accepts any exactly certified strict improvement. Values in unmerged pull requests are not bars.

partial_wins.statement: Line: an explicit strategy certified strictly better than the exact expected meeting time of Han et al.'s published 15-Markovian strategy (recomputed exactly from the strategy given in their paper), even if the gain is smaller than 1e-4.

Five locations: an explicit symmetric strategy for n = 5 whose exactly computed expected meeting time is below that of FSD(theta) at its best theta, computed exactly by the verifier (the 2026 paper gives only a lower bound on FSD's improvement for n >= 5).

verification_method: Line: write the joint process of the two agents (each agent's automaton state or path index, the relative position, and the relative orientation, which is +1 or -1 with probability 1/2) as an absorbing Markov chain; meeting is absorption when the relative position hits 0, at an integer time or by crossing within a step. For a k-Markovian strategy, enumerate all pairs of paths in the support for both relative orientations, compute the per-round meeting probability and the expected time spent, and solve the renewal equation exactly, as in the worked examples of arXiv:1805.03351 (Alpern's strategy gives exactly 5). Test the verifier on Alpern's 5 and on the simple 2-Markovian strategy (exactly 7) first. Locations: build the chain over (round position, both players' visit histories modulo the random labelings) and compute the expectation exactly; test on Anderson-Weber for n = 3 and on FSD's closed-form improvement for n = 4.
status_checked: 2026-10-14; historical source check from supplied batch A material. Current sources were not re-fetched during preparation.
angles: Push k: Han et al. stopped at k = 15 (2^15 paths per agent) with fractional quadratic programming in 2008, and their conjecture that R is about 4.25 suggests the k-Markovian optimum keeps falling with k. Optimise distributions over paths for k = 16 to 24 with sparse supports, many random starts in parallel, and exact re-evaluation of every improvement.

Search over richer strategy classes than renewal-type k-Markovian ones: small randomized automata whose next path depends on the previous round's path; the September 2026 paper's truncated-chain and weak-peek frameworks give ready-made finite-state machinery for evaluating them.

For four locations, start from FSD and Weber's 2009 12-step block idea and optimise over correlated tours across several rounds, guided by negative eigenvalues of the matrix of pairwise meeting times, as Weber did; exact evaluation is a finite sum over pairs of label sequences (15,852 pairs for Weber's block strategy).

Lower bound: Han et al.'s bounds rest on absorbing Markov chains, fractional quadratic programming and semidefinite programming (their abstract); a larger relaxation solved in floating point and rounded to an exact rational dual certificate is the route to a checkable improvement.
pitfalls: Published bounds are rounded to four decimals; a claim within 1e-4 of 4.2574 needs an exact comparison with Han et al.'s actual strategy (partial win p1), not with the rounded number.
Conventions differ: n-location values depend on whether players can meet at time 0 (as in arXiv:2604.02058) or only from time 1. State the convention and compare like with like.
Floating-point evaluation of a strategy is not a certificate; use exact rationals or rigorous intervals, and include meetings that occur mid-step on the line.
Strategies must be symmetric: both agents use the same rule, with independent randomness and independent orientations; any rule that assigns roles (wait-for-mommy) is excluded.
The unknown-distance line problem (best symmetric ratio 13.926, Klimm, Sagnol, Skutella and Tran, SODA 2022) is a different cell and is not covered by this criterion.
Active field: Georgiou's and Klimm's groups both published in 2026; re-check arXiv before claiming.
